en: Now, thus far in this course, we already saw
a couple of algorithms and a couple of
different time complexities. I also showed
you this
asymptotic analysis approach that allows you
to derive the
time complexity of an algorithm on your own.
And we most often saw something like O
or O thus far. Throughout the course, we'll
also see a couple of other time
complexities, of course.
Now, there are 2 important takeaways here.
The first important takeaway is that we're
really only interested in this asymptotic
analysis. We're only interested in the big
picture, in the nature of an algorithm. We
don't care if it theoretically is O
or O
or anything like that. For us, it's
interesting that it's O so that there is a
linear relation between n
and the time this algorithm takes. And it
doesn't matter to us how steep that linear
graph would be. It doesn't matter to us if
the runtime grows twice as fast as n
or anything like that. We just care about
the general trend. That's the first
important thing.
But in addition,
you also should reach a state where you
don't need to count all operations, but
where you simply look at a function like
this and you quickly see which kind of time
complexity we have here. It's of course good
if you're able to identify best and worst
cases since that is also something you
should be capable of doing.
But more importantly, you should be able to
relatively quickly see what the worst or
average case runtime is, what Big O notation
we would use.
And there are a couple of very easy
rules, or at least hints towards which time
complexity we have for which kind of
algorithm.
Thus far, we mostly saw O
and O.
We also had O), but that is kind of similar
to O, just a bit more specific than just O.
But these are the 2 general kinds of time
complexities we saw thus far.
O, as you learned, is linear time
complexity, which means a higher n
leads to an increase in runtime, and the
increase in runtime is linear.
And O, on the other hand, means that the
runtime is not really affected by a higher
n.
Now, to quickly identify
which kind of time complexity which function
or algorithm has,
there is a simple rule. You typically have
an O kind of algorithm if you find a single
loop in there. With single loop, I mean that
an algorithm could have multiple loops but
no nested loops.
For example, here for get_min, we quickly
see that there is a loop in there.
Now if we had a second loop after this first
loop, we would still have linear time
complexity, just something like 2n or
anything like that.
If we had a nested loop in there though, so
a loop in the loop,
then I can tell you it will not be linear
time complexity. Then it would probably be
quadratic time complexity, but we'll see
this later. So a loop, a single loop without
any nested loops, is a great hint towards
linear time complexity.
On the other hand, if you have a function
without any loops and without any other
function calls inside of it, there is a very
high chance you are dealing with constant
time complexity like down there.
So these are 2 easy rules which are easy to
memorize. Have a loop without any nested
loops and of course also without any nested
function calls, so without any function
calls inside of the function,
then you're dealing with linear time
complexity most likely.
Have a function where you have no loop and
no nested function calls, then it most
likely is constant time complexity.
Now, cases like our is_prime
function here, our is_prime algorithm where
we actually had O of square root of n,
there the square root part is nice to have.
Of course, it's more specific than just O of
n, but if you would say that this algorithm
is O of n, it would also not be horrible. We
just can be a bit more specific here. So the
takeaway here simply is that if you have a
loop, it most likely is linear time
complexity, but it then is worth taking a
closer look at that loop to see what's going
on in that loop. And you should check how
your iterator, your exit condition variable,
changes with every iteration and what your
exit or your runtime condition is.
And if you then see something strange like
that you shrink that number up to which you
loop,
or that you
don't just add 1 to the iterator after every
iteration but you add a bigger number— if
you have something like this, chances are
you're better off than linear time
complexity because you won't go through all
the numbers up to a number, but you instead
shrink the number of iterations you're going
through simply by changing the exit
condition and/or by by how you manipulate i
after every iteration. So that's the second
step. The first step is that you look for
loops and then if you have a loop, as a
second step, analyze that loop and see if
there is something strange about it that
influences the number of iterations and
maybe decreases that number so that you're
not on linear time but you're better than
that.
